podcast.body: The original recording of "Revolution" was used in a highly controversial 1987 Nike commercial for their "Air Revolution" line of shoes. This use of what was considered "a sacred call to action" by John Lennon to sell shoes sparked immense public outrage. The ad agency, Wieden+Kennedy, chose the Beatles' song over an alternative by the Georgia Satellites. The licensing deal, worth between $7 and $10 million, was negotiated with Michael Jackson, who had acquired a significant portion of the Beatles' publishing catalog in 1985, and Yoko Ono, who supported the deal to expose her late husband's music to new generations. The remaining three Beatles (Paul, Ringo, and George) "went ballistic," suing Nike for $50 million, though the matter was settled out of court. The campaign significantly boosted Nike and became one of advertising's most influential spots, marking a turning point in commercial music licensing. "And what's more, this sacred call to action that John Lennon wrote in the 1960s was being used to sell shoes."

podcast.body: This faster version of "Revolution" was featured as the B-side to the single "Hey Jude." It represents the band's approach to offering significant content on their flip sides, diverging from the industry norm of placing less important tracks there. "Hey Jude, on the A side, came with the fast version of Revolution on the B side."

podcast.body: This iconic Beatles song was controversially sold for use in a 1987 Nike sneaker commercial for half a million dollars. The sale was approved by Michael Jackson, who owned the publishing, and reportedly by John Lennon's widow, Yoko Ono. The media widely criticized this move as the "ultimate sellout of baby boomer musical iconography." "The sale of the Beatles song Revolution, to Nike for a 1987 sneaker commercial."
